01 — Background

I've been building things on the internet for more than 20 years. Eventually I realised the interesting bit wasn't really the website.

I started as a web developer, spent years working in ecommerce and consulting, and eventually realised the interesting bit wasn't really the website. It was what happened after somebody showed up. Did somebody reply? Did they follow up? Did the customer know what to do next?

Big businesses build systems for all of that. Small businesses usually have the owner trying to remember who they quoted last Tuesday while they're halfway up a ladder. I’d already seen that world growing up around my dad’s bicycle shop. That’s where good opportunities disappear.

A personal note

These days I prefer building things that solve boring, expensive problems — the sort nobody thinks much about until they realise how much work is slipping through the cracks.

The expensive part isn't having a broken follow-up process. It's continuing to send good leads through it.

03 — Where the money leaks
Someone enquires while you're working. You'll reply later.
Someone gets a quote. You'll chase them when you get a minute.
Someone says they'll think about it. They're now somewhere in WhatsApp, your inbox, a notebook or your head.
None of that feels particularly serious at the time. Until you add up what those jobs were worth.
04 — The point
You might not need more leads. You might just need to stop losing the ones you've already got.
